cards.explanation: The answer is False. Eli, the priest at Shiloh, had two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, and the text says they were wicked men who had no regard for the LORD or for the custom of the priests with the people (1 Samuel 2:12-13). The custom was real, and they walked right past it. I've seen a cookie sheet get more respect than that.

The answer is a three-pronged meat fork. Verse 13 says the servant of the priest comes with it while the meat is boiling. Three prongs means three chances to grab something. Picture a guy showing up to your cookout with his own personal harpoon.

The answer is himself. Verse 14 says the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. The servant plunged that three-pronged fork into the pot, and whatever came up on it went to the priest. I'd say that's a pretty handy setup for him.

The answer is False. Verse 14 says, “This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.” Not some of them, not the unlucky ones, all of them. If you came to Shiloh with a sacrifice, friends, you were in the fork's path.

The answer is raw. The servant tells the man to give the priest meat to roast, because the priest “…will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.” (1 Samuel 2:15). So the man's sacrifice is still being prepared and the servant is already placing an order. That's like walking into my bakery and asking for the dough before I've even turned on the oven.

The answer is that he says to give it now or he takes it by force. The servant says, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!” (1 Samuel 2:16). The man had only asked for the fat to be burned first. He got a threat in return, which is a rough way to end a conversation.

The answer is True. Verse 17 says, “…the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD…” Severe is a strong word, and the text picked it. Whatever anybody else made of the fork and the threats, the LORD saw it as a serious matter.

The answer is contempt. Verse 17 says, “…they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.” That offering belonged to the LORD, and the text names exactly how these young men treated it. Contempt means looking down on something.

The answer is a little robe. Verse 19 says his mother would make him a little robe each year and bring it to him. Hannah, Samuel's mother, makes it herself. Every year, a fresh one, which tells me somebody keeps growing.

The answer is three sons and two daughters. Verse 21 says the LORD attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. That's five more children, on top of Samuel. A full table, friends, and I bet a loud one.

The answer is False. Eli says to his sons, “No, my sons; it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people.” He says he hears about their wicked deeds from all these people (1 Samuel 2:23). People were talking, and it wasn't a compliment.

The answer is that no one can step in for him. Eli says, “If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25). He asks it as a question, and he leaves it right there. I think he wants his sons to feel how big that is.

The answer is False. The text says, “But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death.” (1 Samuel 2:25). Eli spoke up, and his sons would not listen. It's a heavy moment.

The answer is in favor with the LORD and with man. Verse 26 says, “And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.” Right next to all that trouble with Eli's sons, Samuel is growing. It's a bright spot in a dark chapter.

The answer is priest. In verse 28 the LORD says, “…out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest…” He selected Eli's father out of all the tribes of Israel, so I think that was a big honor. That makes what happens next even harder to hear.

The answer is sons. The LORD tells Eli, “You have honored your sons more than Me…” (1 Samuel 2:29). That's a hard thing for a father to hear, and the text doesn't blur it. Eli's sons were the ones he put first.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.” (1 Samuel 2:30). The first half matches, but the text says disdained, not overlooked. Two groups, friends, and two very different outcomes.

The answer is that they will both die on the same day. The LORD says, “They will both die on the same day.” (1 Samuel 2:34). Hophni and Phinehas are Eli's two sons, and this is the sign He gives Eli. I think this one hurts, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “He will do whatever is in My heart and mind.” (1 Samuel 2:35). After all that trouble with Eli's sons, this priest is described very differently. He's called faithful, and that word carries the whole verse.

The answer is priestly. Verse 36 has them pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.” Everyone left in Eli's house will come and bow down for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread. Priestly is the word they use.
